fixes.explanation: I see why you'd go there, friend, but the man says the opposite. He asks the LORD, "Do not hide Your face from me in my day of distress." and then adds, "answer me quickly when I call." That's a man who wants an answer quickly, not one who says to take His time.
That's it, baker. He says, "I even forget to eat my bread." His heart is afflicted and withered like grass, he says. I think the man is carrying something heavy, and the verse shows it.

Right on. He says he's like a desert owl, like an owl among the ruins, and like a lone bird on a housetop. I think those pictures say he feels all alone. He also says he lies awake, and I bet that's a lonely stretch for him.

Birds do fly, so I see the pull of that one. But the man never says anything about home or flying off. He says he is like a lone bird on a housetop, and I think that picture is about being by himself.

I can see why, since the man started out begging God not to hide His face. But after the "But," he says, "…You, O LORD, sit enthroned forever…" He doesn't call Him far off or silent anywhere in this verse.
That's right, friend. The man tells the LORD, "…it is time to show her favor…" He also says, "…the appointed time has come." That's the opposite of saying her time hasn't come yet.

Yes, rebuild. Just before that, the man says God's servants delight in her stones and take pity on her dust. Then he says, "For the LORD will rebuild Zion…" The LORD is the one who builds her back up.

That's right, friend. Verse 17 says, "He will turn toward the prayer of the destitute; He will not despise their prayer." The LORD turns toward those prayers, and He doesn't despise them. That comes right after the man says the LORD has appeared in His glory.

That's what he says. "Let this be written for the generation to come, so that a people not yet created may praise the LORD." He's asking for it to be written for people who haven't even been born yet. I think that's a generous thing to do.

Yes, friend. The text says the LORD gazed out from heaven to earth "…to hear a prisoner’s groaning…" He looked down from the heights of His sanctuary to do it. God looked down to listen to someone who was groaning, and that's the whole picture.
Nothing in these verses has God listening for boasting, friend. He gazed out from heaven to earth "…to hear a prisoner’s groaning…" A groan is what the verse puts on His list, not a boast.

That's the word. The LORD looked down "…to hear a prisoner’s groaning, to release those condemned to death…" The verse puts hearing the groaning and releasing those condemned to death side by side, and I think that's beautiful.

That's right. The prayer ends with, "The children of Your servants will dwell securely, and their descendants will be established before You." After all those hard verses, it lands on safe and steady. The man says it just after saying God remains the same and His years will never end.
